titre: Broken on the wheel in a public square, cleared three years later
accroche: Toulouse, March 10, 1762: a Protestant merchant is broken on the wheel for the alleged murder of his son. On March 9, 1765, eighty judges declare him innocent.
contenu_vulgarise:
On October 13, 1761, on the ground floor of the family shop on rue des Filatiers in Toulouse, Marc-Antoine Calas, twenty-eight, is found dead, hanged. His father Jean, a sixty-three-year-old Protestant merchant, sees a suicide. Rumor tells another story: the son was about to convert to Catholicism, and his Protestant family supposedly killed him to wash away that shame. Nothing establishes it, but the rumor is enough. The capitoul David de Beaudrigue, a municipal magistrate in charge of the inquiry, questions Jean and his son Pierre as early as October 15, then has the whole family arrested.

## A justice that does not stop to check

On November 18, 1761, the capitouls sentence Jean Calas. He appeals to the parlement of Toulouse, which confirms the sentence on March 9, 1762, by eight votes to five, without any weapon or direct witness being produced. The next morning, Calas is tortured to make him name accomplices: he confesses nothing. That same afternoon, he is broken on the wheel in Place Saint-Georges, displayed on the wheel, strangled, and his body is burned. Between the confirmation of the sentence and its execution, a single day has passed. No rule of the kingdom then provided for an ordinary appeal against a parlement ruling in a criminal matter: once the sentence was handed down, it was carried out.

Voltaire, living at Ferney, at first skeptical, changes his mind after meeting Pierre, one of the Calas sons who had taken refuge in Switzerland, who persuades him of his father's innocence. Convinced, he writes in 1763 his *Traité sur la tolérance* (*Treatise on Tolerance*), which takes the affair as its starting point, and launches a letter-writing campaign to the highest courts of Europe to obtain a review of the trial. This is not a judicial remedy: it is public opinion manufactured from outside the system that condemned Calas, to force a higher body, the King's Council, to intervene.

## An innocence with no culprit

On June 4, 1764, an assembly of eighty judges of the King's Council quashes the ruling of the parlement of Toulouse for procedural defect and orders a new trial. On March 9, 1765, the chambre des requêtes de l'Hôtel (the royal household's court of petitions) rehabilitates Jean Calas and his family unanimously. Louis XV grants the widow and children a pension of 36,000 livres. The capitoul Beaudrigue, whose inquiry had served as the foundation of the entire accusation, is dismissed on February 25 of the same year.

No one, however, is ever found guilty of the death of Marc-Antoine. What the King's Council established was not who killed him: it was that nothing allowed his father to be accused. The rehabilitation of 1765 clears without elucidating, which is already, on the scale of Ancien Régime criminal law, a considerable shift: guilt pronounced by a sovereign court ceases to be taken for granted merely because it was pronounced. More than a century before Émile Zola published “J'accuse” for another man judged on a rumor rather than on facts, the Calas affair already fixes the mechanism: a trial closed by a local court reopens only if someone outside it makes enough noise for a higher authority to look at the file again.

repere.texte: On March 9, 1765, the chambre des requêtes de l'Hôtel unanimously quashes the 1762 conviction and rehabilitates Jean Calas and his family; Louis XV grants them a pension of 36,000 livres.

carte.punch: Broken on the wheel a day after his sentence was confirmed, cleared three years later
carte.idee: In 1762, Jean Calas is broken on the wheel in Toulouse for the alleged murder of his son, with no proof and no possible appeal. Voltaire's campaign brings in the King's Council, which quashes the sentence in 1764. In 1765, eighty judges rehabilitate him, never identifying a culprit.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The text Voltaire wrote out of the Calas affair to argue against religious intolerance.

quiz.question: Why could the trial of Jean Calas be reopened only after his execution, and not before?
choix: Because the parlement of Toulouse itself asked for a review after doubting its verdict
Because no ordinary appeal existed against a parlement ruling, and only an outside intervention by the King's Council could quash the sentence
Because the law required a one-year delay between conviction and execution, during which Voltaire was able to act
Because Marc-Antoine Calas was found alive in 1764, which automatically voided the murder charge
quiz.explication: The parlement of Toulouse had issued a final ruling, enforceable without delay: Calas is executed the day after its confirmation. No ordinary appeal existed at the time; it took the King's Council, a body outside the parlement, to quash the sentence for procedural defect in 1764, before the chambre des requêtes rehabilitated the family in 1765. Marc-Antoine's body was never found alive: he died on October 13, 1761.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What rumor circulates in Toulouse after the death of Marc-Antoine Calas, and pushes toward the arrest of his family?
choix: That he had gambling debts to Toulouse creditors who supposedly killed him
That he was about to convert to Catholicism and that his Protestant family supposedly killed him to wash away that shame
That he had argued publicly with his father the day before his death
That he planned to denounce his father to the authorities for illegal religious practice
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The rumor holds that Marc-Antoine was about to convert to Catholicism and that his Protestant family killed him to wash away that shame. Nothing establishes it, but it is enough to have the whole family arrested.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What convinces Voltaire, at first skeptical, of Jean Calas's innocence?
choix: Reading the complete trial record, sent by the parlement of Toulouse
A statement from the capitoul Beaudrigue acknowledging an error in the inquiry
A letter from the widow Calas addressed directly to Ferney
His meeting with Pierre, one of the Calas sons who had taken refuge in Switzerland
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the meeting with Pierre Calas, a refugee in Switzerland, that persuades Voltaire of his father's innocence and leads him to write his Treatise on Tolerance in 1763.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the rehabilitation of Jean Calas by the chambre des requêtes establish on March 9, 1765?
choix: That Marc-Antoine Calas did commit suicide, as an eyewitness finally confirmed
That a servant of the Calas family is the real culprit in the murder
That nothing allowed his father to be accused, without ever identifying who killed Marc-Antoine
That the capitoul Beaudrigue himself fabricated false evidence against Calas
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The rehabilitation clears without elucidating: it establishes that nothing allowed Jean Calas to be accused, but no one is ever found guilty of the death of his son Marc-Antoine.
